De Regno Christi
day REG-noh KRIS-tee
proper noun (a treatise of Martin Bucer)
Latin, “On the Kingdom of Christ”; the treatise written by the Reformer Martin Bucer in 1550 for the young King Edward VI of England, on the reform of church and commonwealth under Christ's kingship.

📖 Biblical Definition

De Regno Christi (“On the Kingdom of Christ”) is the major treatise of the Strasbourg Reformer Martin Bucer, written in 1550 during his English exile and presented to the young King Edward VI, setting forth a comprehensive program for the reform of both church and commonwealth under the kingship of Christ. Bucer argued that Christ is King over all of life, and that a Christian realm should order its worship, its church discipline, its laws, its care of the poor, its marriage and education, in conformity to the law and gospel of God. The dictionary treats the work as a witness to the Reformed doctrine of the kingship of Christ. Its great truth is biblical: the Father has set His King upon His holy hill, declared that He must reign till He hath put all enemies under His feet, and bidden His people pray, “Thy kingdom come, thy will be done in earth.” Christ's lordship is not confined to a private spiritual sphere but extends over every realm of human life. The dictionary honours Bucer's vision against the modern privatizing of faith and the Radical Two-Kingdoms error that would shut Christ out of the public square. Yet it also marks the work's limitations and the cautions of later Reformed reflection: Bucer's program leaned heavily on the godly magistrate to enforce reformation, a Constantinian and theocratic confidence that the Baptist tradition, with its insistence on liberty of conscience and the spiritual nature of Christ's kingdom, would temper. The dictionary thus commends the central truth—the universal kingship of Christ—while reading the magistrate's role through the corrective of the 1689 Confession's fuller doctrine of conscience and the church's spiritual power.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Martin Bucer's 1550 treatise for Edward VI on the reform of church and commonwealth under Christ's kingship; honoured for the truth of Christ's universal lordship (Psalm 2:6; 1 Corinthians 15:25), tempered by the Baptist doctrine of conscience and the spiritual kingdom.

DE REGNO CHRISTI, proper noun. [Latin, “On the Kingdom of Christ.”] Martin Bucer's 1550 treatise for Edward VI.

It sets forth the reform of church and commonwealth under Christ's kingship.

Its truth: Christ reigns over all of life (Psalm 2:6; 1 Corinthians 15:25).

Honoured against the privatizing of faith and the Radical Two-Kingdoms error.

Tempered by the Baptist doctrine of conscience and the spiritual nature of the kingdom.

📖 Key Scripture

Ps 2:6 — "Yet have I set my king upon my holy hill of Zion."

Mt 6:10 — "Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven."

1 Co 15:25 — "For he must reign, till he hath put all enemies under his feet."

Ps 110:1 — "The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the cautions are Bucer's heavy reliance on the godly magistrate to enforce reform, tempered by the Baptist insistence on liberty of conscience and the spiritual kingdom.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the universal kingship of Christ. Bucer's great and biblical truth is that Christ reigns as King over all of life—over worship, law, family, education, the care of the poor—and that no realm of human existence lies outside His lordship. The Father has set His King on Zion, and He must reign till every enemy is under His feet. The dictionary honours this against the modern privatizing of faith and especially against the Radical Two-Kingdoms error, which would confine Christ's rule to an inner spiritual sphere and shut Him out of public life.

Yet the dictionary marks the limitations of Bucer's program and the cautions of later Reformed reflection, without disparaging the man or the truth he served. Bucer leaned heavily on the godly magistrate to compel reformation by the sword of the state—a Constantinian and theocratic confidence shared by much of the magisterial Reformation. The Baptist tradition, and the 1689 Confession after it, while affirming Christ's universal kingship, tempered this with a fuller doctrine of liberty of conscience and the spiritual nature of Christ's kingdom, which advances by the Word and Spirit, not by the magistrate's coercion. The dictionary commends the kingship of Christ that De Regno Christi proclaims, while reading the magistrate's role through that corrective.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin De Regno Christi, “On the Kingdom of Christ”; regnum (kingdom, reign) names the universal rule of Christ the treatise sets forth.

expand to see more

Regnum, Latin, “kingdom” or “reign,” the rule of Christ over all.

Written by Martin Bucer in 1550 during his exile at Cambridge.

Presented to the young King Edward VI of England.

A program for reform of church and commonwealth under Christ's lordship.

Read through the corrective of conscience and the spiritual kingdom.

Usage

"The teacher cited De Regno Christi for the truth that Christ reigns over all of life."

"He honoured Bucer's vision against the Radical Two-Kingdoms confinement of Christ's rule."

"She tempered the treatise's reliance on the magistrate with the Baptist doctrine of conscience."
